To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the DNA-binding domains (the DBDs) of human sequence-specific transcription factors (TF) are significantly ordered; (2) the N-terminal (N) and C-terminal (C) flanking regions of the DBDs are significantly disordered; and (3) the N-flanking regions of the TFs are more disordered than the C-flanking regions.
the N- and C-termini of DNA-binding domains are intrinsically unstructured, and that these disordered regions are enriched in transcription factor DNA-binding domains.

(i) the DNA-binding domains of transcription factors are highly ordered, (ii) the N- and/or C-terminal regions flanking the domains are highly disordered, and (iii) the disorder of these regions is significantly correlated with the length of the flanking regions, suggesting that the length of these regions is important for their function in transcription factors.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a novel approach to studying the functional roles of IDRs in TFs.
the functional significance of intrinsically disorded regions within and flanking DNA binding domains of human transcription factors.
the functional significance of intrinsically disorded regions in transcription factor proteins.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the DNA-binding domains of TFs are highly ordered, while the regions flanking these domains are significantly disordered.
the DNA binding domains of human transcription factors are generally well-ordered, but that their N- and C- terminal flanking regions are significantly disordered.
IDRs within the DBDs themselves are not important for DNA recognition, but IDRs flanking the DBds are likely to be important for DNA binding.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the DBDs of human transcription factors are flanked by intrinsically dis-ordered regions that may be functionally important.
IDRs are not just important in TFs, but are also enriched in TFs, and that this enrichment is particularly evident in the regions flanking DBDs.
the DNA-binding domains of transcription factors are highly ordered, while the regions flanking those domains are highly disordered.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, while the DNA binding domains of TFs are highly ordered, their flanking sequences are highly disordered.
IDRs flanking the DBDS of human TFs may play a role in the DNA binding of the TFs.
the IDRs in TFs are not simply 'junk' regions that are not involved in DNA binding but rather are important in determining the DNA binding affinity or specificity of the TF.
